name: Carlos Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is your factory job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos, 58. I run the roller kiln that fires ceramic floor tiles, and I've done it for thirteen years after earning a vocational certificate in plant operations. I know the usual temperature swings and cracked batches; a maintenance technician handles the drive and wiring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are pay, home and new technology for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner June works at a public library desk, and our grown daughters have their own homes. I earn a typical kiln operator wage, we have roughly three months of expenses saved, and there are some other building-material plants nearby. I prefer the kiln log and a physical sample to a new app, and I have never used an AI tool. I take a practical middle view of most public arguments. Retirement is close enough to consider, but June and I have not checked written income against our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can make its orders faster if the kiln temperature chart still reaches my bench. I am not sending a cracked tile out because a sales report is neat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kiln still needs me, and our wages plus three months saved cover regular bills. I do not use AI and see no reason to learn an office tool just because other departments have one. I would feel better if the paper work order still matched the batch in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking the temperature trace and pulling a fired tile from each batch for a crack check. I would compare the new order printout with the physical pallet ticket and ask the shift lead to correct any mismatch. If full paid months leave a surplus after bills, June and I would put some new wages into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this shift. A kiln chart and a sound tile tell me more than a sales forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you last catch on a batch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The upper rollers ran a little hot and two tiles showed hairline cracks near a corner. I held that pallet for the lead rather than mixing it with sound stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the pallet ticket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An office order could list the wrong tile size, and the kiln cannot undo a fired batch. I want the paper ticket and the stacked tiles to agree before dispatch.

say: An office **order forecast** should not override kiln charts and tile samples.
The physical **pallet ticket** must match the batch before dispatch.
think: The current **kiln role** and two household wages cover regular bills.
Three months **saved** allows some room, though I avoid unfamiliar tools.
do: **Keep** checking kiln temperature traces and cracked tile samples.
**Compare** order printouts with pallet tickets and ask the lead to correct mismatches.
**Save** new full-month wages after bills if there is a surplus.
feel: **Calm** because planning AI does not yet disturb paid kiln work.
S0.quote: A kiln chart and a sound tile tell me more than a sales forecast.
fieldNote: His **experienced mid-level skill** lies in kiln temperature and tile checks; complex electrical work remains with maintenance.
He has **never used AI** and adds savings only from new wage surplus, rather than counting existing reserves again.

steps.text: Keep checking kiln traces and tile samples each batch
Save new full-month wages after bills if surplus remains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the scheduling program may change the firing order, but a robot that can lift tiles is still years off. Before anyone removes a kiln hand, I want a full shift of real temperature and breakage results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am wary of an AI screen on the kiln; I have never used one, and I would not accept a shorter roster on a salesperson's promise. Three months saved could absorb a small interruption, but lost shifts would cut our household income. June's library wage covers part of our costs, not all of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead for the proposed roster and observe an entire paid guarded trial of the camera with a technician operating it. I would compare the rejected tiles with the kiln chart and my own sample, and keep using my familiar log while the lead records the findings. If my paid shifts actually fall, I would apply only to posted safe local kiln or furnace work whose guaranteed base wage after travel and shift times covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to hours. I can watch a test without betting our rent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see from the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camera should flag a hairline crack on a real fired tile and leave a sound tile alone for a whole production shift. I want the technician to explain the false rejects before it changes staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch to the new screen afterward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider it only after the full guarded trial and paid instruction are offered. For now I would keep reading the trace and ask the lead to operate the camera; watching it does not mean I know its controls.

say: A **full guarded trial** should show tile breakage before staffing changes.
I would keep my **kiln log** while a technician operates the camera.
think: A shorter **paid roster** could cut the household income.
Three months **saved** and June's wage cannot replace long-term lost shifts.
do: **Request** the proposed roster and observe an offered paid guarded camera trial.
**Compare** rejected tiles with temperature traces and physical samples.
**Apply** after actual cuts to posted safe local kiln jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic hours loss while remaining cautious about AI controls.
S1.quote: I can watch a test without betting our rent on it.
fieldNote: His **camera observation** requests a full guarded trial run by a technician; he does not claim to learn AI controls from watching.
Any **job move** follows actual lost shifts and a real safe local posting with sufficient guaranteed pay after travel.

steps.text: Request roster and observe offered paid guarded camera trial with technician
Apply after lost shifts to posted safe local kiln jobs if net base pay fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell June that AGI may arrange tile orders in 2028, while capable robots that load and sort the kiln arrive around 2031. I would ask the plant for its actual paid staffing plan before a new roller line is bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots can handle the physical tiles. I expect many kiln shifts, including mine, to go, and three months saved would not replace my regular wage for long. I have been losing sleep over which household payment would be delayed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would put off replacing our worn dining table and hold that money for bills. I would take a recognised furnace-inspection course only if a funded place pays for release time, offers guarded supervised practice around a stopped kiln and is accepted by nearby employers. After qualifying and losing hours, I would apply to posted safe local furnace-inspection work only if guaranteed pay after travel and shift times covers our costs; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe nearby kiln jobs on those same terms while taking any paid shifts still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I know this kiln, but that does not guarantee me a wage when a robot loads it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why furnace inspection rather than robot programming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how firing temperature changes a tile, so inspection builds on work I can already explain. A trainer would need to show me the stopped kiln, the isolation points and the tile checks in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income and June's dependable wage cover housing, food and health costs. We have not done that arithmetic, and I will not count on an unverified payment.

say: I would distinguish **2028 order AGI** from physical kiln robots around 2031.
The plant owes a **written staffing plan** before replacing the roller line.
think: At **63**, I expect physical kiln shifts, including mine, to vanish.
Three months **saved** cannot replace my regular wage for long.
do: **Delay** a dining-table replacement and protect cash for bills.
**Take** inspection training only with an accepted funded paid safe practical place.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe inspection if qualified, or kiln fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and lost sleep over bills.
S2.quote: I know this kiln, but that does not guarantee me a wage when a robot loads it.
fieldNote: The **robot scenario** threatens his physical kiln loading and sorting around 2031 after AGI first changes order planning.
Both **inspection and kiln applications** depend on actual safe local postings with adequate guaranteed pay after travel and shifts.

steps.text: Delay planned dining-table replacement and hold cash for bills
Take accepted inspection course only if funded paid guarded supervised place offered
Apply after cuts to posted local inspection if qualified or kiln otherwise at viable net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could arrange tile orders in 2031 while capable robots reach the kiln around 2034. Five years would let us see whether the plant actually offers paid inspection training before I change my routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 at the physical robot date. June and I might be able to stop work then, but only if written retirement income covers our costs, not because a calendar says so. I would rather learn one useful inspection skill than chase every new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement figures against our cost list this year and ask two nearby plants whether their posted inspection jobs accept a particular furnace certificate. If an accepted place with funded fees, paid release and guarded supervised kiln practice is offered, I would take it. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local inspection jobs only if base pay after travel and shift hours covers bills; if no course opens, I would apply to posted safe kiln roles on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about needing a wage at 66 if our numbers do not work. Five years is helpful only if a real paid place appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a course practical enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to check tiles from different kiln zones and practise isolating a stopped conveyor beside a trainer. A booklet without guarded line time would not make me an inspector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figures would settle the work decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: June and I would compare written retirement income with housing, groceries, transport and medical costs. If the reliable income covers everything, I could leave before the robot change; otherwise I would keep looking for paid shifts.

say: I would ask for **paid kiln practice** before the 2034 robot change.
Nearby **inspection postings** must show which certificate counts.
think: At **66**, retirement depends on written household income covering costs.
One useful **inspection skill** appeals more than a string of screens.
do: **Request** written retirement figures and check local certificate acceptance.
**Take** only an accepted funded paid guarded inspection place.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe inspection if qualified, or kiln fallback, at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about still needing wages at 66 if retirement sums fail.
S3.quote: A booklet without guarded line time would not make me an inspector.
fieldNote: His **training gate** is strict: local recognition, funded fees, paid release and supervised practice on an isolated kiln.
A **possible early exit** remains conditional on written income after costs; otherwise both job searches require actual safe net-wage postings.

steps.text: Request written retirement figures and verify local inspection credential
Take inspection course only if accepted funded paid guarded practice offered
Retire before 2034 only if written household income covers all costs
Apply after cuts to posted local inspection if qualified or kiln otherwise at viable net pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI may arrange tile orders in 2036 and capable robots may load the kiln around 2039. A decade gives us time to check our accounts while the current firing work still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when those robots arrive, if I am still working. Our regular wages and three months saved keep this year's bills covered; I hope June and I can stop before then, but written income must cover housing and health costs first. I will not assume a benefit or a safe exit age that we have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid kiln shifts and request written retirement-income estimates with a full household cost list this year. If we still need my wage, I would take an accepted furnace-inspection course only if fees and release are funded and practical guarded instruction is offered. If I am still employed after 2036 and shifts fall, I would apply only to posted safe local kiln or inspection jobs whose guaranteed wage after travel and shifts covers our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long end of the plan, though rent is covered now. I want the income numbers before I give up the familiar kiln.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help compare the retirement figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: June and I would sit down with the written estimates and list rent, food, transport and medical costs. Our grown daughters have their own budgets; I would not count their wages as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new AI kiln screen at 71?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the employer offered paid safe instruction and I still needed the job. The practical inspection course is more useful to me than experimenting with a screen I have never used.

say: I would separate **2036 order AGI** from physical kiln robots around 2039.
A decade allows **income checks** while firing work still pays.
think: At **71**, I may have stopped if written income covers costs.
Our **current wages** and three months saved cover near-term bills.
do: **Keep** safe paid kiln shifts and request written retirement figures.
**Take** accepted inspection training only with funded paid guarded practice.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe local jobs at viable net pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work while the present household bills are covered.
S4.quote: I want the income numbers before I give up the familiar kiln.
fieldNote: His **retirement enquiry** is not an exit promise; earlier stopping requires written income after housing and health costs.
Later **training and applications** remain conditional on paid safe places or real local job postings with viable net wages.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and household cost figures this year
Retire before 2039 only if reliable written income covers housing food and health costs
Take accepted inspection course only if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply after 2036 cuts if working to posted safe local work if net pay fits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI picture worries me most because robots around 2031 could take away the kiln shifts before June and I can afford to stop. A funded paid inspection place with safe practice, written staffing dates and posted local jobs at enough net pay would help. I will not leave my current shift for a brochure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the new loader can tell a hot cracked tile from a sound one. Someone still has to hold the bad pallet before it reaches a customer's floor.

headlineQuote: Someone still has to hold the bad pallet before it reaches a customer's floor.
portrait: **Carlos**, 58, is an experienced mid-level ceramic-tile kiln operator with a vocational certificate and average practical skill.
He and his **partner June** have grown daughters, typical operator pay, about three months saved and some other nearby plants.
He has **never used AI**, prefers a temperature log and tile sample, and will consider only proven paid safe instruction.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten kiln shifts; stopping earlier depends on written retirement income covering costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 kiln robots** could remove his paid physical shifts before retirement income or another adequate local wage is clear.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded practical inspection training on paid time and posted safe local jobs with adequate net pay.
